title: Aurora Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Aurora wells have a 50 ft median depth, but the middle half ranges from 29 to 610 ft. See yields, costs and buyer risks.
h1: What Aurora Well Records Tell You Before You Buy
intro_html:
Aurora sits on the plains, but well conditions within five miles vary sharply. Colorado DWR records show 2,201 permitted wells, with 1,192 reporting total depth and 246 reporting pump yield. The local record includes shallow wells and deep Denver Basin wells, so a nearby address is useful evidence but not a guarantee for your lot.

For a buyer, the important questions are practical: how far a driller may need to go, how much water the well can produce, and what the complete installation may cost. The records also point to groundwater-quality issues and the need to confirm septic, building, and water-right requirements before closing.

sections.heading: Aurora well depths range from shallow to very deep
sections.html:
The recorded median depth near Aurora is 50 feet, but that number hides a wide spread. The middle half of reported wells runs from 29 to 610 feet. About 62% are under 100 feet, while 26% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record reaches 2,360 feet.

That spread matters when you request a drilling bid. A shallow neighboring well may support a modest estimate, while a property tapping Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock could require a much deeper hole. Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, Denver aquifers, and Dawson aquifers. All of the named aquifer records are Denver Basin wells, but the exact formation and local geology still need to be checked for your parcel.

sections.heading: Most Aurora wells report useful production, but test the lot
sections.html:
Among the wells with a recorded pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 65% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 34% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures describe reported wells, not a promise for an unbuilt well. Yield depends on the formation, completion, pump, and test method. Ask for the neighboring well permits and well-completion reports, then have a driller evaluate the proposed location. A yield test and an adequate storage setup are more useful than relying on the area median alone.

sections.heading: Recorded Aurora water levels are shallower in newer measurements
sections.html:
The current recorded median static water level is 27 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 12 to 350 feet. That range is broad enough that one nearby well may not represent another. Static water level is also not the same as the level while pumping, so a pump test remains important.

The decade series does not show a simple dropping water table in these records. Median measured depth to water was 242 feet in the 1980s, 30 feet in the 2010s, and 14 feet in the 2020s. The measurements come from different wells and locations, so they should not be read as a controlled trend study. Treat the series as context, and confirm present conditions with recent neighboring records and an on-site well evaluation.

sections.heading: Aurora permit history shows long, continuing well activity
sections.html:
Permit activity began early and continued through the newest recorded permit year, 2025. The records show 49 permits in the 1950s, 43 in the 1960s, 137 in the 1970s, 289 in the 1980s, 333 in the 1990s, 401 in the 2000s, 243 in the 2010s, and 184 in the 2020s.

Most recorded uses are monitoring wells at 46%, followed by domestic or household use at 27%, stock at 5%, and irrigation at 4%. That mix matters: a large number of permits does not mean every well serves a home. The most active drillers in this record are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.), and Don Eastwood Drilling Inc. (Eastwood, Don). Confirm current licensing and availability before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: A median-depth Aurora well may cost $8,500 to $15,500 finished
sections.html:
For Aurora’s Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,500 to $3,500. That is only the hole, not a functioning household water system.

A finished installation with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $8,500 to $15,500 at the median depth. The wide depth distribution is the reason not to use that figure as a fixed bid. A 600-foot or deeper well can materially change drilling and equipment costs. Get the proposal in writing and ask what happens if the hole is dry, the yield is low, casing or grout requirements change, or trenching and electrical access are more difficult than expected.

sections.heading: Check Aurora water quality, septic clearance, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Water quantity is not the only issue. Mapped environmental data within about 10 miles includes 172 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 21 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove contamination at a particular property, but it is a reason to review site history, well records, and laboratory testing before relying on the water. Historic mine features are not mapped in this area.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk still exists even though the recorded yield distribution is favorable. Confirm casing, grout, pump depth, and construction details. Before building, verify the well permit’s allowed use and coordinate the well location with septic and leach-field setbacks, access for drilling equipment, electrical service, and the proposed house. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan or other water-right requirement may apply; the permit and current DWR requirements control.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Aurora, Colorado?
faq.a: The recorded median well depth within five miles of Aurora is 50 feet. The middle half runs from 29 to 610 feet, and 62% are under 100 feet. However, 26% are 600 feet or deeper, with the deepest record at 2,360 feet. Nearby well depth is useful for planning, but local geology can change the bid substantially.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Aurora?
faq.a: The drilling model for Aurora uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $2,500 to $3,500. A complete well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,500 to $15,500. Deeper wells, difficult access, and construction changes can move the final price higher.

faq.q: How much water do Aurora wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 65% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 34% report more than 15. These are existing reported results, not a guarantee for a new well, so request a yield test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Aurora?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 172 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 21 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well through a qualified laboratory, review nearby environmental history, and retest after construction or if water quality changes.

faq.q: Do I need to check water rights before building near Aurora?
faq.a: Yes. A Colorado DWR permit controls the well’s allowed use, and domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring permits do not all provide the same authority. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan or another water-right requirement may apply. Review the permit, well location, septic plan, and building proposal with the appropriate Colorado water professionals before closing.
